Use Supabase as your comprehensive backend solution.

## Introduction

Building a web application is a lot of moving pieces. After all, what the user interacts with is just the surface of the iceberg, so to speak. 

Maybe admitting this next bit will brand me as an imposter, but I have to be honest and say that while I'm fairly comfortable with digging around in the frontend, I've always felt a tad intimidated by backend infrastructure. Some of the reason being that traditionally, those moving pieces were generally discrete, meaning that you had juggle a lot of different tools and services without a unified platform to help you manage them.

Enter **[Supabase](https://supabase.com/){target="_blank"}**: A comprehensive backend-as-a-service (BaaS) platform that provides a suite of tools to help you oversee all the moving pieces — from your database tables, to ready-made ways to read and write those tables, to user authentication, to functions that perform tasks when a row changes, and more. So incredibly user-friendly, that a self-professed backend novice like myself managed to cobble together a solution that does exactly what I wanted it to do.

Nostalgic for the websites of the last millennium, I used Supabase to build a retro-inspired [guestbook application](/samples/content-engineering/personal/guestbook/) with some modern touches: anti-spam measures, an admin dashboard gated by Google OAuth 2.0, and email notifications powered by Gmail API.

## The Data API reads and writes the tables

When I wanted the page to show the comments, I did not have to invent a web address for "get the comments" and another for "save a comment." Supabase already has those addresses. They call the whole set the Data API.

If you open the project, go to Project Settings, and select Data API, you will see an API URL. It ends in `/rest/v1`. That ending is the front door to the tables. A table here is just the place a kind of information lives, the way a sheet in a spreadsheet holds one kind of list.

In the guestbook, a helper called `createClient()` in `src/lib/supabase/server.ts` opens that door. It uses the project address, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, and a public key called the anon key. The anon key says which project I mean. It is not a master key. The database still decides what that caller is allowed to see. Under the hood, asking for a table becomes a normal web request to `https://<your-project>.supabase.co/rest/v1/<table>`.

Reading the board is `getPublicCommentsPage` in `src/app/actions/comments.ts`. This is the actual request:

```typescript
supabase
  .from("comments_public")
  .select("id, display_name, body, created_at, updated_at", { count: "exact" })
  .order("created_at", { ascending: false })
```

I left the email address out of that list on purpose. Visitors see a name, a message, and a time, newest first. `comments_public` is a window onto the real comment list that simply does not include the email column.

Saving a comment is `submitComment`. It first checks that the note is not empty or too long, that it is not rude, and that this person has not posted too many times. Only then does it write the name, the email, and the message into the private `comments` table.

`loadAdminComments` is the version on the dashboard. It asks for that private table, email included. Editing, deleting, and marking a comment read (`updateComment`, `deleteComment`, `setCommentRead`, and `setCommentsRead`) aim at that same private table. If you are not an admin, the database refuses. Those refusals are row rules: instructions saved on the table about who may read or change each row. I do not have to remember to repeat that check on every screen. Postgres, the database itself, checks before it hands anything back or lets a write through.

The rest of the app uses that same door.

The settings row is one record, `guestbook_settings`, with the comment length, the speed limit, and how many notes fit on a page. `loadGuestbookSettings` in `src/lib/loadGuestbookSettings.ts` reads it. `saveGuestbookSettings` in `src/app/actions/settings.ts` writes it back, and only after it has checked that the signed-in person is an admin.

Poem hearts do not let the browser write the heart table. `getDeskHeartSeed` in `src/lib/actions/hearts.ts` reads two public count windows, `poem_heart_counts` and `poem_heart_total`. Liking a poem calls a small database function, `toggle_poem_heart`, and `poem_heart_state` answers whether this visitor already liked it. A function call is still the Data API. It goes to `/rest/v1/rpc/<name>` instead of `/rest/v1/<table>`. Signing in as an admin uses that same kind of call: `resolveAdminSession` in `src/lib/adminAuth.ts` calls `ensure_admin_role`.

The admin address list is the one the browser is not supposed to see. The mail function reads it with a server key, in `loadAllowlist` at `supabase/functions/_shared/allowlist.ts`. The docs chatbot does the same kind of thing for its own notes. In `src/app/docs/chat/route.ts`, the server saves a conversation in `docs_chat_session` and each turn in `docs_chat_message`, again with a key that stays on the server.

## Google OAuth 2.0 stamps the admin role

Signing in with Google tells me who a person is. It does not tell me they should be allowed to run the guestbook. Anyone with a Google account can click the button. I keep a short list of admin email addresses, called `admin_allowlist`. If the account is not on that list, I sign them back out.

The login page is `/admin/login`. After Google sends the person back, a function called `ensure_admin_role` looks up their address and writes a small note onto the login: `app_metadata.role` set to `admin`. That note sits where the visitor cannot edit it. When the account is first created, a database hook reads the list. Later, a check named `is_admin()` trusts only that note. A session, by the way, is just the site remembering that this browser already signed in.

I only run this check on the admin pages. Everyone else can sign the book with no account at all.

- If there is no admin session yet, they are sent to `/admin/login`.
- If they sign in and the note does not say admin, they are signed out and sent home with `?admin_error=1` on the address, so the page can show an error.
- If they are already signed in as an admin, they go straight to the dashboard.

If I ever move the dashboard off `/admin`, the same check follows whatever path I put in `NEXT_PUBLIC_GUESTBOOK_ADMIN_PATH`. The Google setup steps are in [Prerequisites](https://beck-chan.vercel.app/docs/prerequisites){target="_blank"}.

## Edge Functions mail on a write

I did not want to sit on the dashboard waiting for a new comment. Supabase can run a small program in the cloud whenever a row changes. They call these Edge Functions. The database taps the function on the shoulder (that tap is called a webhook), and the function sends the email. I can moderate from my inbox. When I want quiet, one on/off switch, `FLAG_NOTIF`, stops the mail and leaves the functions where they are.

I have two. `notify-admins` covers changes to comments, settings, poem hearts, and the admin list. `on-user-created` covers a brand-new account. Both ignore the tap unless it carries a shared password, `NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, so a stranger on the internet cannot trigger the mail. Both also stay quiet unless `FLAG_NOTIF` is on. The people who receive the mail are the addresses on the allowlist. The function reads that list with a server key the browser never sees.

The message I actually read is the new-comment email. The function fills in a short template and sends it with the Gmail API. If someone edits a comment, I only get mail when the name, the email, or the text changed. A behind-the-scenes timestamp does not bother me.

How I turned this on is in [Enable Notifications](https://beck-chan.vercel.app/docs/notifs){target="_blank"}.

## Rate limits live in Postgres

Leave a comment box wide open and a script can fill the board in a minute. I needed a speed limit that would still be there after a restart, and that would agree no matter which copy of the site answered the request. So the counters live in the database, rather than in the short-term memory of one running program.

By default a visitor can leave one comment every five minutes, and two in a day. I can raise those numbers in the guestbook settings.

`submitComment`, the same function that saves a note, spends one of those chances. It does not store the visitor's raw internet address. It stores a scrambled version of it, so the limit can tell people apart without keeping a readable address in the table. The counting tool is called `rate-limiter-flexible`. The browser cannot write those counters. Only the server can.

The docs chatbot has the same kind of limit, for a different reason. Every question costs a call to Gemini, the model that writes the reply. I did not want one browser to use up that allowance. Questions are counted in a table called `docs_chat_limits`: five an hour, and ten a day, again from a scrambled internet address.

## pgvector searches the docs

The docs are long, and searching for the exact words someone typed misses questions asked a different way. `pgvector` is an add-on for Postgres that lets me store a list of numbers standing in for the meaning of a chunk of text. Those numbers are called an embedding. Gemini creates them, and I keep them in a table called `docs_section`, next to the words they came from.

When someone asks the chatbot a question, that question becomes the same kind of list of numbers. Postgres looks for the chunks whose numbers are close, which is a way of saying the meaning is close. It also does an ordinary word search. The chat keeps the few pages that do well on either test, and Gemini may only answer from those excerpts. The reply includes links, so you can go read the pages yourself.

On the public version of the site, only pages I have marked public are searched. The chatbot cannot quote my private notes.

The visitor's browser never reads `docs_section` directly. The chat page on the server does, with a key that stays on the server. I wrote up how I built that in the [chatbot build](https://beck-chan.vercel.app/docs/bot-build){target="_blank"}.

Those same tables are the catalog in [Build API documentation with Scalar](../api/index.qmd). The comment path, speed limit included, is what [Automate tests with Cucumber and Playwright](../cucumber/index.qmd) checks. The number on the page is [Implement hit counters with PostHog](../posthog/index.qmd).
